children: The Bahamas' biggest teachers' union said on Friday it was prepared to take "industrial action" as talks continue with government officials over higher pay and union leaders look to secure a meeting with the Prime Minister Philip Davis.

The warning raises the prospect of a strike, though no date has been set, and adds pressure on Davis' newly re-elected government as it confronts fresh labor unrest in schools just days after some 50,000 state school students returned to class.
The Bahamas Union of Teachers is seeking a 20% salary increase over three years.
Union President Belinda Wilson told members to "have your walking shoes ready" as she awaited a response from the government's lead negotiator.
Over 1,400 union members rejected a government pay proposal on April 15, Wilson said, without detailing the offer.
The Bahamas Educators Managerial Union, which represents some 90% of school administrators, went on a separate strike on Tuesday but was ordered back to work the same day by the Supreme Court.
About 3,700 teachers are employed in primary and secondary schools across the country, according to World Bank data.
Education Ministry official Keenan Johnson and Labor Minister Pia Glover-Rolle both declined to comment.
